evidence_level: associated (matched comparisons adjusting for prior attendance, five states; causal evidence null)
pathway: Regular participation (30 or more days a year, best over two or more years) in 21st Century Community Learning Centers and similar after-school programs is associated with slightly fewer school-day absences than matched non-participants with similar prior attendance.
model_match: Not used for credit. Applies only to programs that track each participant's days attended and report school-record attendance for regular attenders (30+ days) against a comparison group. A program's own participants-only change, or the state 'share under 90 percent who improved' measure, does not count.
typical_effect: About 0.5 to 3.4 more school days a year for regular participants (Texas, New Jersey, Washington, Rhode Island); median center effect d = 0.14 across 779 Texas centers, with wide spread. That is about 0.3 to 1.9 percentage points of attendance rate, so it moves the 90-percent share only for students near the line.
caveats: Selection into regular attendance is only partly handled by matching on prior attendance. The after-school meta-analysis (Kremer et al. 2015) and the randomized trials (Gottfredson et al. 2010; After School Matters, Hirsch et al. 2011; national 21st CCLC evaluation) found no reliable attendance effect, so this must never be worded as 'raises attendance'. Most state reports come from one evaluator (AIR); Westat's Texas site-level study is the independent check. Philadelphia grantee studies are correlational; an arts 21st CCLC in Philadelphia found no difference. Test-score effects are null or negative at low dosage (keep L-12).
rationale: Answers Severin's 21st CCLC question directly: there is a consistent, small, adjusted association across at least two independent evaluators and five states, which meets the associated bar, but the strongest designs say it is not shown to be causal. L-44 currently rests on one Providence study and is rejected because A2.5 is an output; keep the not-for-credit status and the caution, but record the association so partners know what can honestly be said.

evidence_level: B (meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies plus randomized trials, null)
pathway: Offering or attending a general after-school program, including 21st Century Community Learning Centers, did not reliably raise school-day attendance in randomized trials or in a meta-analysis of controlled studies.
model_match: Not used for credit. Bounds P-01 and any after-school logic model that claims attendance gains.
typical_effect: Meta-analytic mean attendance effect small and not significant; randomized trials show no treatment-control difference.
caveats: Program attendance in the trials was often sporadic. State 'percent of students under 90 percent who improved' figures (Pennsylvania 2023-24: 66 percent improved) have no comparison group and reflect regression to the mean; they never qualify.
rationale: The strongest designs on the question Severin raised are null. The map should say so explicitly in its own row, not only inside caveats, because the logic-model checker needs a 'do not claim' entry for after-school -> attendance.

evidence_level: A for the messaging model (now replicated at scale, including rural and federal trials)
pathway: Personalized messages to families about their own child's absences (mailings, texts, teacher-written postcards) correct parents' underestimates, and their children then miss fewer days.
model_match: Repeated, personalized messages naming the child's own absences or missed learning, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. A one-time letter at the 90-percent threshold, a standard legalistic truancy notice, or general family events do not qualify.
typical_effect: Across replications: absences down about 2 to 6 percent (0.2 to 0.5 days in 47 rural districts at about 4 dollars per student; 1.9 percent across six district trials); chronic absence lower in the federal K-5 texting trial; teacher postcards and grade 1-2 teacher-parent contact also reduced absences.
caveats: Effects are small per student and shrink at scale. A regression discontinuity of a single nudge letter at the 90-percent line found no effect; texts plus home visits in grades 6-11 did not change chronic absence; message content matters (redesigned truancy notices). Partners need record access.
rationale: This is the best-established low-cost S1 lever. New federal (Heppen 2020) and 47-district (Swanson 2026) RCTs replicate L-28; the nulls define the conditions. Top candidate for partner guidance: partners with data-sharing agreements can send these at near-zero marginal cost.

evidence_level: B (single randomized field experiment, negative)
pathway: Perfect-attendance awards did not raise later attendance, and after-the-fact awards lowered it.
model_match: Not used for credit. A 'stop doing' entry for partner guidance and logic-model checks.
typical_effect: Retrospective awards reduced subsequent attendance (size to confirm).
caveats: One California trial in middle and high schools; it says nothing about recognition of improvement or of attendance among peers.
rationale: Many partners run attendance incentives and awards. The only randomized test found harm, which is exactly the kind of 'what not to do' item the guidance needs.

evidence_level: B (single large trial; grades 5-7 only; nulls in high school and in a CIS-delivered trial)
pathway: A trained monitor (Check & Connect) who checks each student's attendance data weekly and follows up with the student and family cut absences for students in grades 5 to 7.
model_match: Check & Connect delivered with fidelity: a trained monitor assigned to each student for two years, weekly review of attendance records, and structured follow-up with student and family, for students in grades 5 to 7. General mentoring (see P-06) does not qualify.
typical_effect: Absences in grades 5-7 down 4.2 days a year (22.9 percent); no effect in grades 1-4; no effect on test scores.
caveats: One Chicago trial. A Texas trial delivered by Communities In Schools and a San Diego high school trial found no attendance effect, so it does not generalize to high school or to substitution for usual case management.
rationale: The strongest mentoring-attendance trial in the set, new to the map (L-23 cites only the WWC dropout report). Keep tight conditions because both replications in older grades were null.

evidence_level: B (randomized trials and a meta-analysis, null)
pathway: School-based, community-based, peer and college-access mentoring did not change school-record attendance in randomized trials.
model_match: Not used for credit. Bounds L-25 (NYC Success Mentors) and any mentoring logic model claiming attendance gains.
typical_effect: Effects near zero (g about -0.05 to 0.05) across trials; meta-analysis effects very small and mostly not significant.
caveats: Exceptions are narrow and listed separately: Check & Connect in grades 5-7 (P-05), education specialists for youth in foster care (P-07), Primary Project in K-2 (P-08). Achievement Mentoring results (Lass et al. 2025) were not checked here.
rationale: L-25's caveat says it 'would move up with a randomized design'; the randomized evidence on general mentoring now exists and is null. Mentoring is one of the most common partner models, so this row prevents overclaiming.

evidence_level: B (single trial)
pathway: An education specialist who mentors and advocates for youth in foster care raised their school attendance.
model_match: A dedicated education specialist for middle and high school youth in foster care, working across school and child-welfare systems (Fostering Opportunities model).
typical_effect: Attendance g about 0.49 (to confirm with sample size and points).
caveats: One Colorado trial; foster-care population only.
rationale: Large effect on records in a meets-standards RCT for a population partners serve; single trial, so suggestive only.

evidence_level: B (single trial)
pathway: Weekly play sessions with a trained paraprofessional child associate for young children with adjustment concerns raised their attendance.
model_match: Primary Project as designed: screened K-2 students, trained child associates, weekly sessions in a school playroom.
typical_effect: Attendance g about 0.31 (sample size to confirm).
caveats: One trial, Northeast US; WWC 'with reservations'.
rationale: Early-grade chronic absence is a Philadelphia priority and this is a paraprofessional model partners could staff; hold at suggestive.

evidence_level: B (one randomized trial plus a one-semester replication; significance of attendance effect to confirm)
pathway: One-to-one literacy tutoring in school combined with regular family engagement raised early-grade school attendance as well as reading.
model_match: Future Forward / SPARK model: paid tutors deliver one-to-one literacy sessions several times a week to K-2 students during the school day, plus a family engagement worker who contacts and visits each family monthly. Delivered in the trial by Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Milwaukee. Tutoring alone (L-05) or family engagement alone does not qualify.
typical_effect: Attendance effect size about +0.20 and foundational literacy about +0.23 in the two-year trial (Evidence for ESSA 'Strong'); WWC extract lists absences g about 0.18 as not significant.
caveats: Milwaukee only; the 2018 and 2021 papers may report one trial; resolve the WWC vs author significance difference before promotion.
rationale: A partner-delivered (Boys & Girls Clubs) model with randomized attendance evidence; the family-engagement component is the plausible attendance mechanism and is a low-cost add-on to existing tutoring.

evidence_level: B (randomized null) with a weaker-design positive
pathway: Daily math tutoring did not change total days absent in the Chicago trials; in Washington DC students were less likely to be absent on days they had tutoring.
model_match: Not used for credit.
typical_effect: Chicago: no significant effect on days absent. DC: 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on tutoring days (7 percent), within-student design.
caveats: The DC estimate is a same-day effect; it may reflect scheduling or displacement and does not show a change in the annual 90-percent share. An earlier Chicago cohort (Cook et al. 2014) may show fewer days absent; confirm.
rationale: Searcher D flagged the DC study as a possible overturn of L-05. It is not: the design is weaker than the RCT and the outcome is day-level. Add it so the map is current and states the distinction.

evidence_level: C+ (two independent quasi-experiments; short programs null)
pathway: Comprehensive summer programs that students attend over several summers are followed by fewer school-year absences.
model_match: Multi-summer programs (students return for two or more summers) combining academics and enrichment, with school-record attendance tracked. One-off camps do not qualify.
typical_effect: Horizons attendance g about 0.15; California program 'substantial' reductions in unexcused absence and chronic absence (sizes to confirm).
caveats: Both are quasi-experiments with selection into returning; a short summer robotics program and a STEM break camp found no attendance effect; summer jobs are in L-70 and L-71.
rationale: Many partners run summer programs; the evidence points to multi-summer continuity as the active feature, which is a no-cost design choice (recruit returning youth).

evidence_level: B (two quasi-experiments: difference in differences and synthetic control; nurse staffing alone null)
pathway: School-based health care that lets students be seen at school (telehealth clinics or nurse-based school health programs) cut absences and chronic absence.
model_match: The partner is the health-care operator of an on-site or telehealth school clinic that treats students during the school day. A nurse position alone, health education, or health-system care coordination does not qualify.
typical_effect: Chronic absence down 2.5 percentage points (29 percent) and 0.8 days with telemedicine clinics in rural North Carolina; absences down 7.7 percent (0.6 days) with elementary telehealth; Hawai'i high school chronic absence lower two to three years after adoption.
caveats: No randomized trial. A full-time LPN alone did not help; the CHECK care-coordination RCT and school asthma education (L-66) were null. Rural and Hawai'i settings.
rationale: Health-system partners run school clinics in Philadelphia; two independent quasi-experiments with records outcomes meet the strong-QE bar, and the nulls give the model-match boundary.

evidence_level: B (single cluster randomized trial, 84 schools)
pathway: Online communities of practice that help school nurses act on attendance reduced chronic absence at low cost.
model_match: A facilitated community of practice for school nurses focused on attendance follow-up; a partner could host or facilitate it.
typical_effect: Lower odds of chronic absence for all students; about 764 to 896 dollars per school.
caveats: One district; the partner role is facilitation, not direct service.
rationale: One of the few randomized, low-cost, staff-practice levers; a training-style intervention matching Severin's 'guidance or training' question.

evidence_level: B (single difference-in-differences study)
pathway: Paid community members stationed along routes to school (Safe Passage) reduced school absence rates.
model_match: A community organization hires and deploys adults on designated routes at arrival and dismissal times.
typical_effect: School absence rate down 0.78 percentage points (about 11 percent).
caveats: Chicago only; school-level outcome.
rationale: A community-partner workforce model with a strong quasi-experiment on the indicator; relevant to Philadelphia neighborhoods with violence near schools.

evidence_level: B for district transportation policy, not a partner link
pathway: Eligibility for a school bus or a full-fare transit pass raised attendance and cut chronic absence, while a fare-free bus for all riders did not.
model_match: Not used for credit: transportation eligibility is a district or transit-agency decision. Partners that help families use passes or routes may cite it only as context.
typical_effect: Michigan: attendance up 0.5 to 1 point and chronic absence down 2 to 4 points for disadvantaged students; NYC middle school: attendance up about 1.5 points (3 days).
caveats: Leon County fare-free buses had negative effects (to confirm); long or complex commutes raise absence (Stein & Grigg; Burdick-Will & Stein).
rationale: Strong designs, but the lever is not partner-run; listing it stops partners crediting themselves for district transport and points to a systems ask.

evidence_level: B (mixed: one RD positive, synthetic control and randomized nulls)
pathway: Changes to how or when school breakfast is served gave mixed attendance results; Philadelphia's own classroom-breakfast trial found none.
model_match: Not used for credit; Philadelphia already provides universal free meals.
typical_effect: Breakfast after the bell: lower chronic absence in a regression discontinuity (size to confirm); no attendance increase in a synthetic control; USDA universal breakfast pilot: confirm null.
caveats: School meal policy, not partner programming.
rationale: Adds the strongest new meal studies so the not-recommended verdict reflects both the positive RD and the nulls.

evidence_level: B (randomized null; quasi-experiment negative)
pathway: Housing subsidies and rapid rehousing for homeless families did not improve children's attendance, and rehousing far from school raised absences.
model_match: Not used for credit. If a partner rehouses families, keeping children in their school of origin with transport is the implied condition.
typical_effect: Usual care did as well or better (randomized site); rapid rehousing increased absence and chronic absence, especially when outside the city.
caveats: One municipality each.
rationale: Directly bears on L-86, which rests on parent-reported absences only.

evidence_level: associated (causal eviction design plus independent longitudinal studies)
pathway: Homelessness and eviction are associated with more school absences; eviction causes more absences and school changes.
model_match: Not used for credit; supports housing-stability goals in logic models as a plausible attendance pathway, not a tested program effect (see P-17).
typical_effect: Homeless students miss about 5.8 more days (Los Angeles); eviction raises absences and lowers graduation (Chicago).
caveats: The causal estimate concerns eviction, not a program; programs that rehouse families have not raised attendance (P-17).
rationale: With the existing Philadelphia KIDS study (V-076), at least two independent longitudinal studies now point the same way; check that De Gregorio adjusts for prior outcomes before promoting.

evidence_level: B, mixed replication (NYC and California positive; Tennessee negative; Massachusetts null)
pathway: Community schools that coordinate health, family and learning services on site cut chronic absence in New York City and California, but not in Tennessee or Massachusetts.
model_match: Unchanged from L-36 (lead agency or coordinator of a whole-school community school sustained for three years).
typical_effect: NYC: chronic absence down 7.4 to 8.3 points; California: about 30 percent lower than matched schools in the first full year; Tennessee: chronic absence rose; Massachusetts Wraparound Zones: no attendance effect; CIS Kalamazoo elementary: attendance up.
caveats: Add the Tennessee increase and Massachusetts null to caveats; reviewers should consider demotion to suggestive if the Tennessee design holds and the California estimate is a relative change from a short window.
rationale: L-36 rests on one city. The new studies both replicate and contradict it; the map must show the mixed record before partners rely on it.

evidence_level: B (two school-level trials and a time-series study, null or marginal)
pathway: Whole-school restorative practices reduced suspensions but did not reliably change attendance or chronic absence.
model_match: Not used for credit.
typical_effect: No significant effect on absences (Pittsburgh RCT; Saint Paul); chronic absence reduction only marginally significant when added to Diplomas Now.
caveats: Suspension effects are real and belong to other indicators' pathways.
rationale: Restorative practice is a frequent partner claim for attendance; the randomized record is null.

evidence_level: B (difference-in-differences and quasi-experiment, null)
pathway: Court-based truancy diversion did not improve attendance once regression to the mean was accounted for.
model_match: Not used for credit; also a methods warning: pre-post gains among students selected for high absence are biased upward.
typical_effect: No program effect (five Minnesota districts); no consistent pattern (grades 7-10).
caveats: Philadelphia's Project Start (2005) found fewer unexcused absences with a community-based court, but matching was on demographics; confirm baseline equivalence.
rationale: Gives the logic-model checker an explicit rule-of-thumb citation for regression to the mean.

evidence_level: B for the school-system practice, not a partner link (one positive RCT, one null RCT)
pathway: School early-warning systems reduced chronic absence in one US trial but not in a Norwegian trial.
model_match: Not used for credit: a school or district data system.
typical_effect: Lower chronic absence after one year (REL Midwest); no effect in Norway.
caveats: Partners can use early-warning data but do not run the system.
rationale: Logged so partner 'early warning' claims are read against system-level evidence.

evidence_level: B (two cluster RCTs; WWC finds attendance effects not significant, Evidence for ESSA rates 'Strong')
pathway: A school-wide social and character curriculum (Positive Action) was followed by lower school-level absenteeism in two cluster trials, but the clearinghouse reanalysis did not find the effect significant.
model_match: Not used for credit until the conflict is resolved.
typical_effect: Authors report absenteeism effect size about 0.19 to 0.20; WWC: not significant.
caveats: School-level outcomes; developer-involved trials.
rationale: Partners deliver Positive Action after school; the map should state why it is not credited for attendance.

evidence_level: associated (two independent longitudinal studies with student fixed effects)
pathway: Playing on a school sports team is associated with fewer absences during the season.
model_match: Not used for credit; school interscholastic teams, not community leagues.
typical_effect: Indiana: large in-season reduction with student fixed effects and lower chronic absence; Cuffe et al.: fewer unexcused absences for boys, offset partly after game days.
caveats: Within-student designs control fixed traits but not season-specific motivation; transfer to partner sports programs is untested.
rationale: With Cuffe (V-122) this makes two independent adjusted longitudinal studies pointing the same way, meeting the associated bar.

evidence_level: C+ (one matched QE positive, one small cluster RCT null, Connecticut LEAP lead)
pathway: Relationship-building teacher home visits were followed by slightly higher attendance in DC; a St. Louis cluster trial found no differences.
model_match: Not used for credit; promote to tested only if the Connecticut LEAP evaluation verifies a matched design.
typical_effect: DC: attendance g about 0.07; Connecticut LEAP: about +4 points (lead).
caveats: Selection of families visited; HOME WORKS! had fidelity problems.
rationale: Home visiting is a low-cost partner practice; the map should cite the REL study that is stronger than the current Sheldon & Jung evidence.

evidence_level: C+ (single staggered interrupted time series, 160 schools)
pathway: Caseworkers placed in schools to help families meet basic material needs were followed by lower chronic absence.
model_match: An embedded human-services or community caseworker at the school connecting families to material supports (Pathways to Potential).
typical_effect: Chronic absence down about 7.9 percent (relative, to confirm).
caveats: No comparison group beyond staggered timing; sponsor-run laundry programs give no qualifying evidence (P-27).
rationale: The first direct test for the new F2.4 code; worth listing at suggestive.

evidence_level: none (sponsor pre-post)
pathway: Claims that school laundry programs raise attendance rest on sponsor-reported pre-post results without a comparison group.
model_match: Not used for credit.
typical_effect: Not estimable.
caveats: Absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect.
rationale: Widely promoted; listing it keeps logic models from citing it as evidence.

evidence_level: B (meta-analyses of controlled studies; heterogeneous models)
pathway: Across many attendance interventions, average effects on attendance are small and vary widely by model.
model_match: Not used for credit; a magnitude benchmark for logic-model checks, not a model.
typical_effect: Pooled g 0.25 (22 controlled US studies to 2018); g 0.09 (13 post-2020 US studies); moderate effects for indicated interventions with high heterogeneity; RCT-only and 49-study syntheses to confirm.
caveats: Pooled sizes mix models; family-school partnership estimates are imprecise.
rationale: Gives the checker a realistic prior: a claimed attendance gain far above g 0.1 to 0.25 should be questioned.

evidence_level: B (randomized trial)
pathway: Conditional cash rewards to families, including for attendance, did not raise elementary or middle school attendance.
model_match: Not used for credit.
typical_effect: Little or no effect on elementary and middle school attendance.
caveats: Welfare sanctions tied to teen attendance (Learnfare, LEAP) raised attendance but are state policy.
rationale: Incentive programs are a common idea for 'what hundreds of programs could do'; the at-scale RCT is null.

evidence_level: B for the school model, not a partner link
pathway: Admission to a career academy or technical high school reduced ninth-grade absences.
model_match: Not used for credit (school model).
typical_effect: Fewer ninth-grade absences (size to confirm).
caveats: School enrollment, not a partner program.
rationale: Lottery evidence that strengthens L-75 beyond one Connecticut study.

evidence_level: C+ (difference in differences, one research team)
pathway: Longer participation in whole-school inclusion programs (Special Olympics Unified Champion Schools) is followed by fewer absences, most for students with intellectual disabilities.
model_match: Unified Champion Schools model with inclusive sports, youth leadership and whole-school engagement.
typical_effect: Size to confirm.
caveats: Dose is chosen by schools; check parallel trends.
rationale: Low-cost, partner-delivered model with a records outcome; a lead for the inclusion code.
